title: Childhood Illnesses & Immunisation
description: Common childhood illnesses, when to seek medical help, the immunisation schedule, and the benefits and concerns.
content_html:
Common Childhood Illnesses

All children will experience illness at some point, and parents and carers need to recognise common conditions and their symptoms. Chickenpox is one of the most widespread childhood illnesses, spreading easily through airborne droplets or contact with the fluid in blisters. It begins with a fever and general malaise, followed within 1–2 days by an itchy rash that starts on the chest or back and spreads. The spots develop into blisters, then crust over. It is most contagious from two days before the rash appears until all spots have crusted. Children should be kept away from pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems. Most cases are mild and self-limiting; calamine lotion, cool baths and antihistamines ease itching.

Measles begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes (Koplik spots — white spots inside the cheeks — appear 2–3 days before the rash). The characteristic red blotchy rash spreads from the face down the body about four days into the illness. Measles is highly contagious and can lead to serious complications including ear infection, pneumonia and, rarely, encephalitis. It is a notifiable disease. Mumps causes swelling of the parotid (salivary) glands on one or both sides of the face, giving a 'hamster cheek' appearance, alongside fever and headache. It can lead to orchitis (testicular swelling) in post-pubertal males and, rarely, meningitis. Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils causing severe sore throat, pain on swallowing, fever, swollen cervical lymph nodes and white patches on the tonsils. It may be viral or bacterial; bacterial tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus requires antibiotics.

Key Fact

Meningitis warning signs in children include: a stiff neck, high fever, severe headache, photophobia (dislike of bright light), vomiting, confusion or drowsiness, and a non-blanching rash (spots that do not fade when a glass is pressed firmly against the skin). A non-blanching rash indicates possible septicaemia — call 999 immediately.

Meningitis and When to Seek Medical Help

Meningitis is one of the most serious childhood illnesses. Bacterial meningitis, most often caused by Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcal) or Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcal), can progress from first symptoms to death within hours. The early signs mimic a flu-like illness, making it easy to miss. As the disease progresses, a distinctive non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash may appear — caused by bleeding under the skin from septicaemia. Parents should be advised to use the glass test (press a clear glass firmly over the rash: if it does not fade, it may be meningococcal disease) and call 999 immediately. Not all meningitis cases produce a rash; the combination of high fever, severe headache, stiff neck and photophobia should prompt urgent medical review regardless.

More generally, parents should seek medical attention if: a child has a high fever that does not respond to paracetamol or ibuprofen; the child is under three months with any fever; there is difficulty breathing; the child is unusually pale, limp or unresponsive; there is a rash or persistent vomiting; the illness is lasting longer than expected; or the parent's instinct tells them something is seriously wrong. Persistent or severe symptoms that do not match a known mild illness should always be checked by a healthcare professional.

The UK routine childhood immunisation schedule is free on the NHS and follows a nationally agreed timetable updated from January 2026. At 8 weeks: 6-in-1 vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib, hepatitis B — first dose), Rotavirus (oral, first dose), MenB (first dose). At 12 weeks: 6-in-1 (second dose), MenB (second dose), Rotavirus (second dose). At 16 weeks: 6-in-1 (third dose), PCV (pneumococcal — first dose). At 1 year (12–13 months): MMRV vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella — first dose), PCV booster, MenB booster. Note: from January 2026 the MMRV vaccine replaces MMR; the Hib/MenC booster has been discontinued for children born from July 2024. At 18 months (new appointment, for children born on or after 1 July 2024): 6-in-1 (fourth dose), MMRV (second dose). From 2 years, annually each autumn: flu vaccine (nasal spray) — the programme continues through primary and secondary school age. At 3 years 4 months: 4-in-1 pre-school booster (diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio). At 12–13 years (girls and boys): HPV vaccine. At 14 years: 3-in-1 teenage booster (diphtheria, tetanus, polio), MenACWY. This schedule protects children from serious diseases at the age they are most vulnerable.

Key Fact

Herd immunity is achieved when a high enough proportion of the population (typically 90–95% for measles) is immune to a disease, so it cannot spread easily — protecting those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns and immunocompromised individuals. Maintaining high uptake rates is essential for herd immunity to hold.

The benefits of immunisation are well established: vaccines have eradicated smallpox globally and near-eliminated polio; MMR vaccination has dramatically reduced measles cases; herd immunity protects vulnerable groups who cannot be vaccinated. Immunisation is free on the NHS, saving families the cost of treatment for serious illness. However, some parents express concerns: minor side effects such as redness, swelling or a mild fever at the injection site are common and short-lived. More serious reactions (anaphylaxis) are extremely rare — approximately 1 in 1 million doses. A now-retracted 1998 study (Wakefield) claimed a link between the MMR vaccine and autism; this has been comprehensively discredited by large-scale studies involving millions of children, and Wakefield lost his medical licence. Despite this, vaccine hesitancy remains a public health challenge, and health visitors play a key role in providing evidence-based reassurance to parents with concerns.
exam_tip_html: When writing about immunisation, always distinguish between individual benefits (protecting the vaccinated child) and population benefits (herd immunity protecting those who cannot be vaccinated). For meningitis questions, name specific warning signs — 'a non-blanching rash' and 'photophobia' score more marks than 'a rash' and 'light sensitivity'. On concerns around immunisation, you may acknowledge parental worries but must also state that the MMR–autism link has been comprehensively discredited.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Common childhood illnesses include chickenpox, measles, mumps and tonsillitis; meningitis is a medical emergency identified by a non-blanching rash, stiff neck, high fever, severe headache and photophobia — call 999 if these signs appear.
  • The UK childhood immunisation schedule offers free vaccines from 8 weeks to 14 years, protecting against diseases including MMRV, meningococcal disease, polio and HPV, and contributing to herd immunity for vulnerable groups.
  • Immunisation's benefits (disease prevention, herd immunity, free on the NHS) far outweigh the risks; the alleged MMR–autism link has been comprehensively discredited by large-scale research.

glossary_terms.definition: A highly contagious viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus, causing a fever followed by an itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters that crust over.
Inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, caused by bacteria or viruses; bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.
A rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed firmly against it, indicating possible septicaemia associated with meningococcal disease — a 999 emergency.
Protection of unvaccinated or vulnerable individuals that occurs when enough of the population (typically 90–95% for measles) is immune, preventing disease from spreading widely.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a warning sign that a child may have meningitis requiring immediate emergency action?
A) A blanching rash that fades when pressed with a glass
B) A mild fever that responds to paracetamol
C) A non-blanching rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass
D) Swollen parotid glands on one side of the face
practice_questions.marks: C) A non-blanching rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass [1 mark]
One mark each for any two of: fever / malaise / itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters / rash that starts on the chest or back and spreads / blisters that crust over. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit of the routine childhood immunisation schedule for the wider community.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the benefit (e.g. 'immunisation contributes to herd immunity'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'when a high enough proportion of the population is immune, the disease cannot spread easily through the community'). A third mark for a further linked consequence (e.g. 'this protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns under 8 weeks, pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals, who are most at risk of serious complications if they contract the disease'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the signs and symptoms of measles. Give one reason why it is important that measles is treated promptly.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): measles begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red watery eyes; Koplik spots (white spots inside the cheeks) may appear 2–3 days before the rash; a red blotchy rash then spreads from the face down the body (2 marks for a description of at least three distinct symptoms including the rash; 1 mark for one or two symptoms only).
Reason (up to 2 marks): measles can lead to serious complications such as ear infection, pneumonia or, rarely, encephalitis (inflammation of the brain), any of which can cause permanent disability or death; prompt treatment reduces the risk of these complications developing (2 marks for a specific, explained reason; 1 mark for naming a complication without explanation). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A parent tells their health visitor that they have decided not to have their child vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella because they have read online that the MMR vaccine causes autism.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the MMR vaccination that the health visitor might discuss with the parent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering advantages (prevents three serious diseases; measles can cause encephalitis and death; mumps can cause orchitis and deafness; rubella is dangerous in pregnancy; MMR contributes to herd immunity, protecting babies too young to be vaccinated) and addressing the parent's concern with accurate counter-information (the MMR–autism claim came from a single retracted 1998 study by Wakefield, who lost his medical licence; large-scale studies of millions of children have found no link between MMR and autism; common side effects are minor and short-lived; anaphylaxis is extremely rare). A conclusion acknowledges that parental anxiety is understandable but that the evidence strongly supports vaccination.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points on each side with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Childhood immunisation programmes have significantly reduced the incidence of many serious diseases in the UK over the past 70 years.

Evaluate the effectiveness of the UK childhood immunisation schedule in protecting children's health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Evaluates the schedule's effectiveness using evidence — smallpox eradication, near-elimination of polio in the UK, dramatic reduction in measles cases following MMR introduction, meningococcal B and C disease reduced since MenB/MenC vaccines. Argues the schedule is comprehensive, free, starts at 8 weeks and continues to age 14, and is informed by up-to-date epidemiological evidence. Challenges this by noting that effectiveness depends entirely on uptake — vaccine hesitancy driven by misinformation (MMR–autism myth) has caused measles outbreaks in areas with low uptake; some vaccines require booster doses to maintain immunity; no vaccine is 100% effective; and the schedule cannot protect against diseases for which no vaccine yet exists. Reaches a substantiated judgement — for example, that the schedule is highly effective overall but its protective value is undermined in communities with low uptake, making public trust and health visitor education as important as the vaccine itself.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more developed points on each side with an attempted conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but mainly one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: At what age does a baby in the UK receive their first dose of the 6-in-1 vaccine?
The MMRV vaccine protects against measles, mumps, rubella and _____.
Herd immunity is achieved when a high enough proportion of the population is immune, protecting those who _____ be vaccinated.
Match each childhood illness to its key distinguishing feature.
right: Itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters spreading from chest
Swelling of the parotid salivary glands

flashcard_questions.q: When is a child with chickenpox most contagious?
flashcard_questions.a: From two days before the rash appears until all the spots have crusted over.

flashcard_questions.q: What are Koplik spots and which illness do they indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: White spots inside the cheeks, appearing 2–3 days before the measles rash.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three warning signs of meningitis.
flashcard_questions.a: Any three of: non-blanching rash, stiff neck, high fever, severe headache, photophobia, vomiting, confusion or drowsiness.
Pressing a clear glass firmly against a rash — if it does not fade, it may indicate septicaemia and 999 must be called.

flashcard_questions.q: At what age is the MMRV vaccine first given in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: At 12–13 months (1 year); the second dose is at 18 months for children born from July 2024.
Protection of unvaccinated individuals when enough of the population is immune, preventing the disease from spreading.

flashcard_questions.q: What proportion of the population needs to be immune to measles to achieve herd immunity?
What four diseases does the MMRV vaccine protect against?
flashcard_questions.a: Measles, mumps, rubella (German measles) and varicella (chickenpox).

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the MMR–autism claim made in 1998 rejected?
flashcard_questions.a: The original study was retracted, its author lost his medical licence, and large-scale studies of millions of children found no link.
An infection of the tonsils causing severe sore throat, fever, swollen lymph nodes and white patches on the tonsils.

flashcard_questions.q: Which vaccine does a 14-year-old receive in the UK that protects against four strains of meningococcal disease?
